newsitem.title: GREECE: Athens stays cool as Balkan conflicts reach border.
newsitem.headline: Athens stays cool as Balkan conflicts reach border.

text.p: Bloody conflicts that have raged through the Balkans for six years spread to Greece's border this week but Athens appeared determined to steer clear of the fight.
Greece has stressed that fighting just inside neighbouring Albania was due to internal political problems and had nothing to do with a large ethnic Greek minority in the frontier region.
"The Albanian problem is a problem of democracy," said Prime Minister Costas Simitis. "It is not an issue related exclusively to Greece and certainly not related only to the Greek minority."
But the minority, living on Greece's doorstep, raises the spectre of ethnic conflicts that have swept the Balkans since 1991 when fighting between Serbs and Croats tore Yugoslavia apart.
Heavily-armed rebels challenging President Sali Berisha's rule fought battles with regular army troops less than 30 km (20 miles) from the Greek border on Wednesday.

The rebels, who want Berisha to quit and hold elections, now control a string of towns close to the border. If Berisha's army is capable of mounting an assault from the north, rebels would have nowhere to retreat to but Greece.
Simitis has been in constant touch with his European Union allies and sent deputy foreign minister Yiannos Kranidiotis to Tirana on Friday to make his point clearly to Berisha.
Kranidiotis will also meet leaders of the Greek community and Orthodox Archbishop Anastassios to stress that the minority must avoid becoming a scapegoat for the conflict in the south.
Anti-government riots swept the port town of Sarande at the weekend, setting off a popular uprising in other towns. Sarande is 15 km (10 miles) from the Greek tourist island of Corfu.
Protests and riots erupted in Albania in January after five popular pyramid schemes collapsed and wiped out the savings of thousands of families.
But since the weekend riots, southern Albania has moved well beyond disgruntled investors and taken on the feel of a civil war, with heavily-armed rebels facing off against army regulars.
The Sarande rebels were the first to clash with units of the Albanian army when four rebels and two soldiers were wounded on Wednesday in the hills above Sarande.
The rebels have seized six tanks and rejected an amnesty offer.
Nervous Greek politicans and analysts have been at pains to point out that this was an Albanian uprising and not a revolt by the Greek minority, estimated at 80,000 to 120,000 people.
The minority has been a source of friction between the two states since the Greek-Albanian border was opened after the fall of 45 years of Stalinism and isolationism in Albania in 1990.

But points of contention abound and any dispute over land or ethnic indentity has explosive potential in the Balkans. Greeks refer to the Albanian border region as northern Epirus, implying it should be joined with southern Epirus in Greece.
Like many other Balkan ethnic groups, some Greeks feel their country was cheated in the regional carve-up during the 1912-13 wars which drove Ottoman Turkey from most of the Balkans.
Efforts by Albania and Greece to ease tensions have faced constant challenges, such as a Greek extemist group called MAVI which staged bloody cross-border raids in 1994.
MAVI, which included ex-army officers, was broken up in 1995 but members got off or were given convictions on illegal arms possession although two Albanian soldiers were killed.
What has disturbed many European Union diplomats has been the proximity of the fighting, 30 km (20 miles) from Greece.

"Greece's problem will be if the Albanian army moves against the rebels. Then Athens may have to stand by while ethnic Greeks are mauled along with everyone else or open its border to a wave of political refugees," a Western diplomat said.
